question: The Galician Government's report of the accident involving a Liberian-flagged vessel that jettisoned its cargo of plastic pellets off the Portuguese coast, causing severe pollution on the Galician coast and other areas of Europe, has triggered an argument between the Portuguese and Spanish governments as to the date of the incident.

As rapporteur for the European Parliament's Committee on Fisheries on the revision of the Flag State Requirements Directive, I would like to ask the Commission for the following public information from the European Maritime Safety Agency (EMSA) in Lisbon: 1.
When did the shipping company report the marine pellet dumping accident?
When did the EMSA report the incident?

Will the Commission add plastic pellets to the maritime safety package’s list of sea traffic pollutants, as requested by the Group of the Greens/European Free Alliance, the group my party in the European Parliament is in? In the wake of this incident, the trilogues constitute the ideal opportunity to consider adding it to the list.
answer: 1 &2. The Commission understands that the incident in question took place on 8 December 2023. Portugal reported the incident to the Union Maritime Information and Exchange System (SafeSeaNet), hosted by the European Maritime Safety Agency (EMSA) on the same day (8 December 2023).

While the Commission does not have knowledge of when the operator informed the Portuguese authorities, it is logical to assume that this was on 8 December 2023. SafeSeaNet provides for the sharing of information between Member States, including the loss of containers at sea and it was duly activated. In this case, the Portuguese report to SafeSeaNet was transmitted to Spain on 8 December 2023.

3 The maritime safety Directives (1) are largely based on the rules and standards established by the International Maritime Organisation (IMO) and focus on their harmonised enforcement within the Union, to ensure that all vessels, irrespective of flag, sail safely and in an environmentally friendly manner within European seas.

Plastic pellets, while not currently considered to be polluting substances within the framework of the International Convention for the Prevention of Pollution from Ships (MARPOL), are a topic of work at the IMO in view of developing possible recommendations and measures to address the environmental risks posed by the transport by sea of plastic pellets.

On this basis, introducing new substantive standards goes beyond the scope of our intended revision of the maritime safety package (2). In anticipation of future regulation on plastic pellets under MARPOL, the provisional agreement for the amendment of the Ship-Source Pollution Directive (2005/35/EC) (3) specifically mentions plastic pellets in its review clause.
